newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Mostar Moslems mourn victim of Croat attack.
newsitem.headline: Mostar Moslems mourn victim of Croat attack.

text.p: Standing at the hillside grave of Sevko Sulejmanovic, you can clearly see Western Mostar -- a place he was forbidden to visit.
Sulejmanovic was shot in the head two days ago for trying to cross over to the Croat-controlled sector of town. He was a victim of nationalist hatred, not in war but in peacetime.
The 66-year-old pensioner was part of a procession of Bosnian Moslems who were attacked by armed Croat men as they attempted to visit a cemetery in the Croat quarter.
A further 22 people were wounded in the bloodiest violence to erupt since the Bosnian war ended in 1995.

Hundreds of Moslems turned out for Sulejmanovic's funeral in eastern Mostar on Wednesday. They stood in silence as his coffin was carried uphill to the top of the graveyard, where victims of the 1993 Moslem-Croat war are buried.

An imam (priest) issued an appeal for calm and led mourners in an Islamic chant that echoed across the ruins of the ancient Ottoman town. During the ceremony, a French helicopter from the NATO-led peace force buzzed low overhead in a show of force meant to deter further violence.
"He went to see his deceased relatives, like everyone else, and he got killed," his niece told reporters afterwards. "The whole world should see what's happening here."
The incident on Monday, coupled with a wave of expulsions of the remaining Moslems from the Croat sector, has brought despair to the people of Mostar.
The Neretva river valley town that once attracted tourists for its graceful bridges is now an infamous symbol of the Bosnian war and "ethnic cleansing".

Three years since the end of the vicious Moslem-Croat conflict Mostar remains strictly divided. Croat hardline nationalists have blocked international efforts to reunify the town and have refused to recognise the authority of a new joint government.
Police on both sides enforce an unofficial border along the former frontline between the Croat and Moslem sectors amounting to an invisible Berlin wall for ordinary people.
Now that tensions have escalated only foreign aid workers, diplomats and NATO soldiers are allowed to cross from one side to another.
Few expect war to break out again in Mostar as long as NATO troops are there to police a peace agreement in Bosnia.
But many Mostar residents say they dread a permanent partition, marked by violence and terror, in which ordinary people would enjoy none of the benefits of peace.
The procession on Monday was headed to a cemetery where Croats and Moslems are buried side by side, killed early in the Bosnian war when the two sides were allied against Serb forces.
A man who said he was a friend of Sulejmanovic described him as a "peaceful man" who only wanted to see his home town return to its centuries-old tradition of co-existence.
"Croats are not bad people," he said. "It's only one percent who are causing trouble."
He said Mostar had a history of mixing religions, marriages and nationalities. "This town has to be unified. The question is not whether it's possible."
"It must be that way, it's the only way. We can't continue like this."
